interactions.label: During obstetric abdominal examination, fundal height is measured from which ana

params.question: During obstetric abdominal examination, fundal height is measured from which anatomical landmark to the uterine fundus?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The umbilicus is a reference point used to correlate gestational age (the fundus reaches the umbilicus at approximately 20 weeks), but it is not the starting point for fundal height measurement.

Correct. Fundal height is measured from the upper border of the symphysis pubis to the highest point of the uterine fundus — a predictable anatomical relationship that forms the basis of clinical gestational age estimation.
The xiphisternum is the landmark the fundus approaches at term (~36 weeks), but fundal height measurement always begins from the symphysis pubis as the fixed lower reference.
The ASIS is a pelvic brim landmark used in orthopaedic and general surgical examination, not the reference for obstetric fundal height measurement.

overallFeedback.feedback: Fundal height is measured from the symphysis pubis to the uterine fundus. The symphysis pubis is chosen because it is a fixed, easily palpable bony landmark that does not change position, making it a reliable baseline for serial measurements.
The symphysis pubis is the fixed lower reference from which fundal height is measured in centimetres, correlating with gestational age in weeks — a simple but powerful bedside tool.

params.question: An intern is evaluating a patient with a suprapubic lump. Using the structured four-phase gynaecological case framework, which of the following is a component of the menstrual history?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mode of previous deliveries (vaginal, caesarean, instrumental) belongs to the obstetric history, not the menstrual history section of the framework.
Gravida and parity form the obstetric formula, which is recorded under the obstetric history — a distinct section from the menstrual history.

Correct. The standard menstrual history covers six components: LMP with exact date, cycle length and regularity, duration and amount of bleeding, intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, and dysmenorrhoea.
Pregnancy complications (gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm labour) are documented under the obstetric history, not the menstrual history.

overallFeedback.feedback: The menstrual history specifically covers: LMP (exact date), cycle length and regularity, duration and amount of bleeding, intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, and dysmenorrhoea. Gravida/parity, mode of delivery, and pregnancy complications all belong to the obstetric history.

Dysmenorrhoea is one of six standard menstrual history components. Clearly separating menstrual from obstetric history within the four-phase framework ensures no element is missed during a systematic gynaecological evaluation.

interactions.label: Most preventable maternal deaths in India occur because definitive surgical care

params.question: Most preventable maternal deaths in India occur because definitive surgical care was unavailable at the treating facility.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is false. The video makes the critical point that most preventable maternal deaths in India result from delayed recognition and delayed referral decisions, not from lack of surgical capability. A woman reaching the operating theatre 30 minutes after diagnosis has a far higher survival probability than one reaching at 90 minutes — the difference is recognition speed, not the availability of surgical care.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The video emphasises that most preventable maternal deaths occur not because definitive care was unavailable, but because the emergency was not recognised early enough or the decision to refer was delayed. Recognition speed — not surgical skill — is the single most important determinant of maternal outcome.

interactions.label: A woman with postpartum haemorrhage has received uterine massage and uterotonics

params.question: A woman with postpartum haemorrhage has received uterine massage and uterotonics. After 15 minutes, the uterus is firm on palpation, but bleeding continues as a steady flow and her pulse remains 118/min. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Continue current management for another 15 minutes since the uterus is firm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A firm uterus alone does not confirm an adequate response. All three parameters — uterine tone, bleeding, and haemodynamics — must improve simultaneously. Waiting further with persistent bleeding and tachycardia risks irreversible haemodynamic collapse.

Correct. Adequate response requires all three signs: firm uterus, bleeding reduced to a trickle, and improved haemodynamics (pulse <100, systolic BP >90, capillary refill <2 seconds). Persistent bleeding and tachycardia at 15 minutes indicate inadequate response, mandating immediate escalation.

answers.text: Reduce the uterotonic dose since the uterus is already firm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Reducing uterotonics when bleeding persists would be dangerous. The firm uterus with ongoing bleeding suggests a non-atonic cause — trauma, retained tissue, or coagulopathy — that requires escalation, not dose reduction.

answers.text: Reassess after 30 minutes to allow more time for the uterotonics to act

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The video specifies a 15–20 minute decision window. Extending to 30 minutes with persistent bleeding and tachycardia significantly increases the risk of irreversible harm — the hallmark of obstetric emergencies is that the window between recognition and harm is measured in minutes.

overallFeedback.feedback: An adequate response requires ALL three signs simultaneously: (1) firm uterus on palpation, (2) bleeding reduced to a trickle, and (3) improved haemodynamics (pulse <100, systolic BP >90, capillary refill <2 seconds). Achieving only one sign while the others remain abnormal at 15 minutes means the response is inadequate — escalate immediately.

Adequate response to PPH first-line treatment requires three concurrent signs: firm uterus, bleeding reduced to a trickle, and improved haemodynamic parameters. If all three are not present within 15–20 minutes, the response is inadequate and escalation is mandatory.
